result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.constraint()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L14065-L14218){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.constraint( weights=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Burt's constraint measures the extent to which ego's contacts are redundant, that is, connected to each other. Higher constraint indicates fewer structural holes and less brokerage opportunity. Lower constraint indicates a network position with more non-redundant contacts, offering greater access to diverse information and control benefits. The constraint of node i's ego network is: `C_i = Σ_j (p_ij + Σ_q p_iq × p_qj)²` where `p_ij` are proportional tie strengths: `p_ij = (a_ij + a_ji) / Σ_k (a_ik + a_ki)` and `a_ij` are elements of the adjacency matrix (edge weights). Time complexity: `O(V × D²)` where `D` is average degree Space complexity: `O(V)` ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of edge attribute to use as weights. If `None`, uses edge weight field. If weights don't exist, treats all edges equally. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store constraint values. If `None`, uses `constraint` as the attribute name. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary mapping node IDs to constraint values. If `False`, stores values as node attributes and returns the Graph for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float | None] or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`, a dictionary mapping node IDs to constraint values is returned. Returns `None` for isolated nodes (undefined constraint). If `return_dict=` is `False`, returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A constraint value close to $1$ says ego's contacts are tightly interlinked, so any one tie is largely redundant with the others: high closure, little room for brokerage. Values approaching $0$ mark the opposite regime: ego's contacts sit in structural holes, disconnected from one another, and information or influence flowing between them must pass through ego. Burt (1992) formalizes this as $c_i = \sum_j \left(p_{ij} + \sum_q p_{iq}\,p_{qj}\right)^2$, where $p_{ij}$ is the share of ego's tie strength invested in contact $j$; the inner sum captures indirect ties routed through mutual contacts $q$, and squaring rewards concentration. The low-constraint positions are the ones network theorists usually care about, since they concentrate the classic structural-hole payoffs: access to non-redundant information, control over what crosses between otherwise separate groups, and the ability to recombine ideas from disconnected clusters. That makes constraint a natural instrument for social-capital studies, innovation research, and any organizational analysis hunting for boundary spanners or entrepreneurial positions. Isolated nodes return `None` because there is no ego network to measure over. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Node "B" brokers between "C" and "D", which aren't connected to each other -- a structural hole that gives "B" a low constraint score, while "A" (connected only to "B") has nowhere else to turn and so shows a much higher one: ::: {#d02b1c00 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Simple network with a broker (B) g = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") # Broker .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("B", "D") # Note: C and D are not connected ) constraints = g.constraint(return_dict=True) b_id = g.get_id_from_label("B") a_id = g.get_id_from_label("A") constraints[b_id], constraints[a_id] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.3333333333333333, 1.0) ``` ::: ::: Node "0"'s two contacts ("1" and "2") are connected to each other, closing off any structural hole, while node "3"'s contacts ("4" and "5") remain disconnected -- giving "3" the lower constraint score: ::: {#d6ad48ff .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Compare dense vs. sparse ego networks g = ec.Graph() for i in range(6): g.add_node(label=str(i)) # Node 0: connects to 1,2 which are connected (no structural hole) g.add_edge(source="0", target="1") g.add_edge(source="0", target="2") g.add_edge(source="1", target="2") # Node 3: connects to 4,5 which are NOT connected (structural hole) g.add_edge(source="3", target="4") g.add_edge(source="3", target="5") constraints = g.constraint(return_dict=True) node_0_id = g.get_id_from_label("0") node_3_id = g.get_id_from_label("3") constraints[node_0_id], constraints[node_3_id] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1.25, 0.5) ``` ::: ::: Edge weights factor into the calculation too -- a strong tie dominates the constraint formula more than a weak one: ::: {#3941409c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=5.0) .add_edge("A", "C", weight=1.0) .add_edge("B", "C", weight=3.0) ) g.constraint(return_dict=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {1: 1.0277777777777775, 3: 2.6180555555555554, 2: 0.703125} ``` ::: :::
